title: Ethos commission math: what agents take
subtitle: Working backward from the S-1 and the 80% agent tier
body:
In my post on why I'm selling Ethos, I said agents get most of each agent sale. Ethos stopped disclosing that split after its IPO, so this post walks through how I estimated it.

Two percentages make this confusing. Agents are paid a percentage of the customer's premium. Their share of Ethos's revenue is a percentage of what Ethos books, which is a different number. Most of the math is converting between the two.

How Ethos gets paid

Ethos doesn't collect premiums. The customer pays the insurance carrier, and the carrier pays Ethos a commission. Life insurance commissions are quoted as a percentage of the policy's first-year premium, and almost all of it comes in the first year. Renewals are small, a few percent a year, and many term products pay none.

Ethos books the full expected lifetime commission as revenue the day a policy activates. That amount is net of expected cancellations. Carriers claw back commission when a policy lapses early, and renewals only come in on policies that stay in force. So a carrier contract that pays 120% of first-year premium could be booked at something closer to 115%.

Agent pay works the same way. Ethos books it upfront, net of the clawbacks it expects to collect from agents on early lapses. That's where Q1's one-time $16.5M charge came from. Policies lapsed less than Ethos expected, so it clawed back less agent pay and had to book more.

The 80% floor

Ethos's agent terms pay producers a fee on the premium the customer pays, minus a small admin fee, for the first 12 months of each policy. Every new producer starts in the 80% tier. Producers with more premium in force can move into higher tiers, but those rates are only shown in an image on the terms page, so I don't know them. If a policy cancels in its first 6 months, the agent repays the whole fee. After 6 months, the agent repays the unearned part.

80% is the base tier, the rate a producer gets even with one client. So I treat it as the minimum an agent earns.

Working backward from the S-1

Before the IPO, Ethos disclosed agent payments as a share of its third-party revenue:

PeriodAgents' share of third-party revenue
202362%
202468%
First nine months 202470%
First nine months 202558%

Those disclosures pin down what Ethos books. Booked commission equals the agent's rate divided by the agent's share. If agents earn at least 80% of premium and their share was at most 70%, Ethos booked at least 80 / 0.70, about 115% of first-year premium. At the 58% share, it's about 138%. So 115% is the lowest number consistent with Ethos's own filings. The 2023 figure is older than these agent terms, so I lean on the 2024 and 2025 periods.

The industry numbers I could find point the same way. Agent forums and commission schedules put first-year term commissions at roughly 70-120% of premium, and final expense whole life at 120% or more. A large distributor on top carrier contracts, earning 100-110% in the first year plus small renewals, lands near 115%. Those sources are anecdotal, but they agree with the S-1 math. My guess is Ethos sits near the low end, around 115%, with agents slightly above the 80% starting tier.

Estimating Q3 2026

Ethos's Q3 release doesn't split agent pay from advertising, but it gives enough to estimate it. Gross profit was $230.8M and contribution profit was $66.4M. The $164.3M difference is the variable cost of acquiring policies: ads, agent payouts and other per-policy costs. Direct revenue was $118.8M and third-party revenue was $116.4M. I subtract my estimate of everything besides agent pay, then divide what's left by third-party revenue.

Costs besides agent payLeft for agentsShare of third-party revenue
Ads at 36% of direct revenue, plus $21.2M other$100.4M86%
Ads at 47% of direct revenue, plus $21.2M other$87.3M75%
All direct costs at 60% of direct revenue$93.1M80%
All direct costs at 70% of direct revenue$81.2M70%

Worst case. The first two rows assume direct sales cost what the S-1 showed: advertising at 36-47% of direct revenue, plus other per-policy costs of about 9% of total revenue. That puts agents at roughly 75-86% of third-party revenue.

Conservative case. On the Q3 call, management said return on ad spend fell modestly year over year as they bought more TV, radio and social ads. So direct sales probably cost more than S-1 levels. The last two rows assume all direct costs ran 60-70% of direct revenue, which puts agents at roughly 70-80%. What's left still includes some other third-party costs, so the true agent share is likely a bit lower within the range.

What it implies

If Ethos still books about 115% of premium, a 70-80% agent share means agents average about 80-92% of premium. That's at or slightly above the starting tier, which fits how I think the tiers work. In the worst case it's 86-99%. The chart uses the midpoint of the conservative case: agents get about 86 points of a 115-point commission, and Ethos keeps about 29. In the S-1 years, with agents at the floor, Ethos kept about 35. Both figures are before Ethos's own costs.

There's another way to get the same Q3 numbers. Ethos could be earning less per policy from carriers. Revenue per policy fell 13% year over year in Q3, to $1,655, and management blamed the mix shifting toward third-party and whole life sales. It's probably some of both.

The S-1 floor and the Q3 estimate come from separate data. Putting them together assumes Ethos's booking rate held steady from 2024-25 into 2026, and the falling revenue per policy says it may not have.

What I can't know

Ethos doesn't split ad spend from agent pay, doesn't publish its higher agent tiers, and doesn't disclose its carrier contract rates. The 2025 10-K and the 10-Qs since the IPO don't give the agent share either. Every path through the math ends in the same place, though. Ethos keeps a minority of each agent sale, and that minority has likely shrunk as the agent channel went from a quarter of revenue to half.

Drew,

Sources

  • Ethos agent terms (80% starting tier, 12-month window, clawbacks)
  • S-1/A, January 2026 (agent payments and advertising ratios)
  • 2025 10-K
  • Q3 2026 earnings release (contribution profit, channel revenue, revenue per policy)
  • Q1 2026 earnings release ($16.5M change in estimate)
  • Q3 2026 earnings call summary (return on ad spend)
  • Industry commission ranges (anecdotal): Insurance Forums, term commission levels, Insurance Forums, term renewals, example compensation schedule
